one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes that the two legislative committees primarily handling the proposed Bangsamoro Basic Law (BBL) both favor peace but use diverse strategies. The House committee headed by Rep. Rufus Rodriguez, voting 50-17, approved the BBL with some amendments but did not revise or delete several provisions that critics claim are unconstitutional because their revision would contravene the government's comprehensive peace agreement with the MILF. The Senate committee headed by Sen. Miriam Defensor Santiago believes that, in addition to passing the BBL, Congress should also amend the Constitution to validate the questionable portions. The congressmen -- swayed no doubt by their meeting with the President a few days ago -- are taking the calculated risk that the bill would survive SC scrutiny, or at least that the Court would not invalidate the entire BBL (but only separable parts), unlike the MOA-AD which was totally scrapped. CJP believes the Senate track is safer and better, for three reasons. First, a constitutional amendment or revision would conclusively solve all the legal objections to the bill -- true, that route takes more time, but as CJP pointed out on Feb 8 ('Saving the peace'), the process can be sped up by Congress tackling its legislative function alongside its constituent function; the whole process can be done within the year if Congress puts its mind to it. Second, constitutional amendments would undergo nationwide debate and plebiscite; the purely legislative route would subject the BBL only to a plebiscite in the Mindanao autonomous region -- but the peace we seek is for the whole country, requiring free and robust national discussion and vote. Third, while BBL would be passed under the present Congress and President, its implementation would be undertaken mostly by the new 2016 president; a purely-legislated BBL would surely be challenged in the SC and given due-process requirements may not be decided within PNoy's tenure; the next president may not be as committed and may not defend it as passionately -- and cases are won or lost because of the prudence and diligence of the parties' presentations. But if the BBL is backed by constitutional changes there would be no challenge to its constitutionality; equally important, the next president would be compelled to implement it in full because it would carry the mandate of the entire electorate, not just of those in the Mindanao autonomous region. POSTSCRIPT -- 'More on arbitration': an internationally-respected arbiter, who requested anonymity (true to their calling), emailed an interesting comment on A383. He explained that Unclos (which created Itlos) has an 'opt out provision' allowing a member like China to 'reject' an arbitration suit; however, China did not expressly invoke this provision in its controversy with the Philippines over the Spratlys -- it 'simply refused to participate.' The question is whether the Itlos panel will construe this refusal as a rejection; if so, PH will probably lose because the tribunal would dismiss for lack of jurisdiction. But if PH hurdles the jurisdictional issue, 'the likelihood is that it will win' because PH is the only one presenting arguments and evidence. The second question: how is the decision enforced against China? The arbiter agreed with CJP that PH would lose moral ascendancy to ask China to honor an unfavorable Itlos decision if PH honors only arbitral decisions it wins (Manila Water) and disobeys those it loses (Maynilad); PH should be consistent in observing the rule of law regardless of outcome. SECOND POSTSCRIPT: the CA's TRO stopping BCDA from evicting CJHDevCo upheld the arbitral decision of the Philippine Dispute Resolution Center Inc. and equally important protected the rights of the innocent bystanders CJP wrote about in A383 -- the locators, condominium owners, and golf-club-share holders who paid CJHDevCo in good faith when the lease was still valid.
